item.title: Self-Hosted Encrypted Swap: LUKS dm-crypt vs Plain dm-crypt vs zram Encryption
item.description:
Introduction

Swap space is a fundamental component of Linux memory management, but its security implications are often overlooked. When a server runs low on RAM, the kernel writes memory pages to swap — including pages that may contain encryption keys, authentication tokens, database connection strings, and other sensitive data. If an attacker gains physical access to the storage device or compromises a cloud provider’s disk snapshot feature, unencrypted swap becomes a goldmine of credentials and secrets.

item.title: Self-Hosted Linux Native Filesystem Encryption: fscrypt vs eCryptfs vs dm-crypt
item.description: Filesystem encryption is a cornerstone of self-hosted data security. Whether you are protecting sensitive configuration files, encrypting home directories, or securing database volumes, choosing the right encryption approach matters. Linux offers three primary filesystem encryption technologies: fscrypt (per-directory native encryption), eCryptfs (stacked per-file encryption), and dm-crypt/LUKS (full block-device encryption).
